A message queue is a data structure used in computer systems to manage the exchange of messages between different processes or threads. In software technology, it's often employed for tasks like handling I/O operations (like reading from disk), managing database transactions, or processing network requests. For instance, when writing an application that reads data from a file, using a message queue can help manage the flow of data as files are read, ensuring that no process blocks while waiting for input. This allows the main thread to continue executing other tasks without being blocked by I/O operations.

A rollback plan refers to a strategy or method for restoring an application or system to its previous state before a change was made. It's like having a backup set of files that can be used if the original data gets corrupted or deleted during a software update or upgrade process. This ensures that users don't lose any work they've done by reverting back to their initial setup.

Sharding in software or technology refers to dividing data into smaller, more manageable pieces (shards) across multiple servers or databases. This allows for better scalability by distributing the load evenly among available resources rather than having all shards on one server. It's useful when dealing with large datasets that can't fit entirely on a single machine.

It's like having an emergency stop button on your computer system that can revert the system back to its previous state if something goes wrong. Rate limiting can be thought of as a traffic light system in a busy intersection. In this case, imagine if all vehicles had to stop at a single signal before proceeding; none could move forward without waiting. Similarly, when something happens too fast (like spam emails arriving), rate limiting ensures that only certain types or quantities pass through, preventing overloading systems.
